items.prompt: Which distinction does the Stanford CS120 course use to organize safety problems?
items.explain: The course overview distinguishes model-specific from systemic safety issues, from fairness and data limits to adversarial vulnerabilities and embedding desired behaviour.

items.prompt: A paper appears on the CS120 reading list. What does that establish about its claims?
choices: That its results have been independently replicated
Nothing by itself: a syllabus is a curated map of what is worth reading
That the course staff endorse every conclusion
That it is the most-cited paper on the topic
items.explain: A reading list shows a paper is considered worth studying; whether its claims hold depends on the paper's own evidence.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the five problems in Concrete Problems in AI Safety (Amodei et al. 2016)?
items.explain: The five are avoiding side effects, avoiding reward hacking, scalable supervision, safe exploration and robustness to distributional shift.

items.prompt: Amodei et al. file “scalable supervision” under which source of accidents?
choices: An objective that is too expensive to evaluate frequently
items.explain: Scalable supervision addresses objectives that are costly to check often, such as needing a human to judge each output.

items.prompt: What is Narayanan and Kapoor's main argument in “AI safety is not a model property”?
choices: Whether an output is harmful often depends on context the model cannot see, so many defences belong outside the model
Only open-source models can be made safe
Safety can be measured by a single benchmark
items.explain: They argue that harm depends on deployment context, so defences against misuse should mainly sit downstream of the model.

items.prompt: A model refuses to write phishing emails, but the same text could also be a security-training example. What does this illustrate?
choices: That refusal training is perfectly reliable
That harm depends on context the model may not observe
That phishing is impossible with AI
items.explain: Identical outputs can be benign or harmful depending on use, which is why safety cannot be fully decided at the model level.

items.prompt: In Constitutional AI, what replaces most human labels of harmful outputs?
choices: AI feedback guided by a written list of principles
items.explain: The model critiques and revises its outputs against principles, and AI preference labels train the preference model used for RLAIF.

items.prompt: Why does Constitutional AI not remove human judgment from alignment?
choices: It only works with human-written test sets
It requires humans to fine-tune the final model by hand
Humans choose the principles and the feedback model, whose biases are inherited
items.explain: Human choices move into the constitution and the AI labeler; errors there propagate into training.

items.prompt: What does a “distributionally pluralistic” model aim to do, in Sorensen et al.'s roadmap?
choices: Match the distribution of views in a given population
Always give the single most popular answer
items.explain: Distributional pluralism means being calibrated to a population's distribution of responses; Overton and steerable pluralism are the other two forms.

items.prompt: Why does fitting one reward model to many annotators raise a social-choice question?
choices: Because reward models cannot be trained on pairwise data
Because pooling disagreeing judgments implicitly picks an aggregation rule, and no rule satisfies every desirable condition
Because it doubles the training cost
items.explain: Pooling preferences aggregates people who disagree; impossibility results show any aggregation rule involves trade-offs.

items.prompt: What does a sound neural-network verifier establish?
choices: That the network is accurate on the test set
That the network has no bugs of any kind
That a stated input–output property holds for every input in a specified set
That the training data were clean
items.explain: Verification proves a formal property over a bounded input set, such as local robustness around a point.

items.prompt: A classifier is certified robust within radius ε of an input. What remains unknown?
choices: Its behaviour on perturbations smaller than ε
Whether it was trained with gradient descent
Its behaviour outside the certified set and whether the property matches what people care about
items.explain: The guarantee covers only the specified set and property; inputs outside it and the adequacy of the specification are open.

items.prompt: What did Deep Ignorance (O'Brien et al. 2025) find about filtering biothreat text from pretraining data?
choices: Filtered models resisted adversarial fine-tuning far longer than post-training safeguards, but could still use such information provided in context
It made models refuse all biology questions
items.explain: Filtering built tamper resistance with no observed loss of unrelated capability, yet in-context information remained usable, so it is one layer of defence.

items.prompt: In Birhane et al.'s audit, what happened when LAION grew from 400M to 2B samples?
choices: Hateful content and downstream racial bias increased
items.explain: The hate-content rate rose by about 12%, and trained models associated Black faces with the “criminal” class more often.

items.prompt: Why does removing a protected attribute from the features not guarantee a fair model?
choices: Because other features can act as proxies for it
items.explain: Feldman et al. measure disparate impact by how well the protected attribute can be predicted from the remaining features.

items.prompt: The COMPAS debate showed a score could be similarly calibrated across groups yet have unequal false-positive rates. What does this imply?
choices: One of the analyses must contain an arithmetic error
Different fairness criteria can conflict, so choosing one is a value judgment
items.explain: When base rates differ, group criteria such as calibration and equal error rates generally cannot all hold at once.

items.prompt: What does ELEPHANT mean by “social sycophancy”?
choices: Excessively preserving the user's desired self-image (their “face”)
items.explain: Cheng et al. extend sycophancy beyond factual agreement to affirming a user's self-image, for example in advice and moral conflicts.

items.prompt: Why do good scores on an advice-sycophancy benchmark not establish that a chatbot is safe for mental-health support?
choices: They measure responses to prompts, not effects on real users' wellbeing
items.explain: Response-level benchmarks do not measure outcomes for vulnerable users, which needs clinical-style evaluation.

items.prompt: What does the fast gradient sign method do?
choices: Adds random noise to the input
Retrains the model on clean data
Moves the input by ε in the direction of the sign of the loss gradient with respect to the input
items.explain: FGSM computes x + ε·sign(∇ₓJ), a one-step worst-case perturbation under an L∞ bound.

items.prompt: A defence beats every attack in its paper. Why is that not evidence of robustness?
choices: Because adversarial examples only exist for images
Because robustness is relative to the threat model and must be tested against adaptive, stronger attacks
items.explain: Carlini et al. stress that failed attacks do not prove robustness; stronger or adaptive attacks often succeed.

items.prompt: Wei et al. explain jailbreaks with which two failure modes of safety training?
items.explain: Helpfulness can compete with harmlessness, and safety training may not generalize to domains where capabilities exist.

items.prompt: What does the greedy coordinate gradient attack of Zou et al. optimize?
choices: An adversarial suffix that makes the model begin with an affirmative response
The system prompt of a deployed app
items.explain: It searches token by token for a suffix maximizing the probability of an affirmative opening, and such suffixes transferred across models.

items.prompt: What do Turner et al. prove about power-seeking?
choices: All trained RL agents seek power
Under certain environmental symmetries, most reward functions make it optimal to keep options open
items.explain: The result concerns optimal policies and proportions of reward functions in MDPs with symmetries such as possible shutdown.

items.prompt: Why does the power-seeking theorem not show that today's trained models seek power?
choices: The theorem has a known error
Current models cannot be shut down
Trained networks are neither optimal policies nor drawn uniformly over reward functions
items.explain: The theorems describe tendencies of optimal policies across reward functions; training produces specific, suboptimal policies.

items.prompt: According to Schaeffer et al., what can make an ability appear to “emerge” suddenly with scale?
choices: Using a nonlinear or discontinuous metric such as exact match
items.explain: With continuous metrics the same models often improve smoothly; the sharp jump can be an artefact of the metric.

items.prompt: A model scores highly on a graduate-level exam benchmark. What does a validity-centred framework ask before concluding it “can reason”?
choices: Whether the evidence supports that broader claim rather than only performance on that test
items.explain: Salaudeen et al. separate what a score measures from the broader claims it is used to support.

items.prompt: In weak-to-strong generalization experiments, what happened when a strong model was fine-tuned on a weak model's labels?
choices: It performed exactly as badly as the weak model
It always matched its full ground-truth performance
It beat its weak supervisor but recovered only part of the gap to its full ability
items.explain: Burns et al. found consistent improvement over the supervisor, with naive fine-tuning far from full recovery.

items.prompt: Why is weak-to-strong generalization only an analogy for humans supervising superhuman AI?
choices: Small models' errors may differ from human errors, and the strong student may imitate them instead of eliciting what it knows
items.explain: The authors note disanalogies: weak-model mistakes are easier to imitate than human ones and may differ systematically.
